A porpoise is a small, warm-blooded sea animal that breathes air through a blowhole on top of its head. It is a mammal, just like you — meaning it gives birth to live young, nurses its babies with milk, and breathes air rather than water. Porpoises belong to the same large group of animals as whales and dolphins.
What it looks like

Porpoises have a compact, torpedo-shaped body built perfectly for moving through water. They are generally small — most species grow between 1.4 to 2.5 metres (roughly 4 to 8 feet) long — and they tend to look stocky and rounded rather than slender.

The most recognizable feature of a porpoise is its blunt, rounded head with no beak. This is the single most important detail to remember, because it is the clearest way to tell a porpoise apart from a dolphin (explained below).

Their dorsal fin (the fin on their back) is usually triangular and upright, somewhat like a shark's fin, rather than curved backward.

Porpoises are typically dark grey or brownish on top and lighter or white on the belly — a pattern common in many sea animals that helps them hide from predators both above and below.
How it's different from a dolphin

This is where most people get confused, so it deserves careful attention.

Porpoises and dolphins are relatives, but they are not the same thing. Think of them like cousins — related, but distinct. Here are the key differences:

  • Head shape: A porpoise has a blunt, rounded head with no snout or beak. A dolphin has a long, pointed snout (beak) that juts forward — the kind you see in cartoons and aquariums.
  • Teeth: Porpoises have flat, spade-shaped teeth (like a tiny shovel). Dolphins have conical, pointed teeth (like small pegs or cones).
  • Body: Porpoises are stockier and more compact. Dolphins are generally more slender and streamlined.
  • Dorsal fin: Porpoises have a triangular dorsal fin. Dolphins typically have a curved or hooked dorsal fin.
  • Behaviour: Porpoises are generally shy, quiet, and solitary or found in very small groups. Dolphins are typically more social, playful, and acrobatic — they are the ones you see leaping out of the water and riding the bow waves of boats.
  • Vocalisations: Dolphins are much more vocal and produce a wider range of sounds. Porpoises are quieter and communicate with high-frequency clicks that are above the range of human hearing.
  • Family: Porpoises belong to the scientific family Phocoenidae. Dolphins belong to the family Delphinidae (among others).

A simple way to remember it: if it has a beak, it is most likely a dolphin. If it has a round, smooth head with no beak, it is likely a porpoise.
Where it lives

Porpoises are found in coastal and nearshore waters — the shallower parts of the ocean near land, rather than in the deep open ocean. They prefer cold to temperate seas. The harbour porpoise, the most commonly seen species, lives in the North Atlantic Ocean, the North Pacific Ocean, and the Black Sea. Some species also live in bays, estuaries (where rivers meet the sea), and occasionally rivers.
What it eats

Porpoises are carnivores — they eat other animals. Their main food is small fish such as herring, sprat, and whiting. They also eat squid and small crustaceans. A porpoise needs to eat a large amount relative to its body size — roughly 10% of its own body weight every single day — because the cold water it lives in demands a lot of energy to keep warm.
How it finds food and navigates

Porpoises cannot see very far underwater, so they rely on a remarkable natural ability called echolocation (also called biosonar). This works like a biological sonar system:

  1. The porpoise produces very high-pitched clicking sounds from inside its head.
  2. These sound waves travel through the water, bounce off objects (fish, rocks, the seabed), and return to the porpoise as echoes.
  3. The porpoise's jaw and inner ear pick up these echoes, and its brain processes them to create a detailed "sound picture" of the surroundings.

This allows porpoises to locate prey, judge distances, and navigate — even in complete darkness or murky water. The clicks porpoises use are at a higher frequency than those used by dolphins, making them even harder for humans to detect.
Social life and behaviour

Porpoises are generally quiet, reserved animals. Unlike dolphins, they are rarely seen leaping dramatically out of the water or playing near boats. They tend to be timid and avoid human contact. They usually travel alone or in very small groups (called pods), though some species occasionally gather in larger numbers where food is plentiful.
Reproduction

Porpoises are mammals, so they reproduce the same way humans do — internally, and they give birth to live young. A female porpoise carries her baby (called a calf) for about 10 to 11 months before giving birth. The calf is born tail-first (to prevent it from drowning during birth). The mother nurses it with rich, fatty milk and the calf stays close to its mother for about a year while it learns to survive on its own. Porpoises reach sexual maturity at around 3 to 4 years of age and can live for 20 to 25 years, though many do not survive that long in the wild.
Species

There are 7 known species of porpoises in the world. A few notable ones:

  • Harbour porpoise (Phocoena phocoena) — the most widespread and commonly seen species; found in the North Atlantic and North Pacific.
  • Vaquita (Phocoena sinus) — the world's smallest cetacean (the group containing whales, dolphins, and porpoises) and also the most critically endangered marine mammal on Earth. It lives only in the northern part of the Gulf of California (Mexico) and there are believed to be fewer than 10 individuals remaining.
  • Dall's porpoise (Phocoenoides dalli) — found in the North Pacific; one of the faster-swimming porpoises, known for the distinctive black-and-white pattern on its body.
  • Finless porpoise — found in Asian coastal waters and some major rivers, and uniquely, has no dorsal fin at all.
Threats and conservation

Several porpoise species are in serious danger. The main threats are:

  • Bycatch — porpoises accidentally get caught and drown in fishing nets intended for fish. This is the single biggest threat to their survival.
  • Pollution — chemicals, plastic waste, and noise pollution in the ocean harm their health and disrupt their echolocation.
  • Boat strikes — collisions with fast-moving boats can injure or kill them.
  • Habitat degradation — destruction of coastal environments reduces their food supply.

Conservation organisations and governments around the world work to protect porpoises through fishing regulations, protected marine areas, and reduction of ocean pollution.
In everyday usage

The word "porpoise" is sometimes used loosely and incorrectly by people to refer to dolphins in general, particularly in older texts or casual speech. This is understandable — they look similar to the untrained eye — but technically, porpoises and dolphins are distinct animals. In precise, scientific, or careful use of language, "porpoise" refers specifically to members of the family Phocoenidae, not to dolphins.
In summary

A porpoise is a small, air-breathing sea mammal with a round, beakless head, a compact body, and triangular dorsal fin. It is closely related to dolphins and whales but is a separate kind of animal. It lives in coastal ocean waters, uses echolocation to hunt fish and squid, and tends to be shy and quiet compared to dolphins. It is warm-blooded, nurses its young with milk, and several of its species are under serious threat of extinction.
